2025.note: Palou won eight races including the Indianapolis 500 and took a third consecutive title, sealing it at Portland with a round still to run. He became the first driver to win the Indianapolis 500 and the championship in the same season since Dario Franchitti in 2010, and at 28 the youngest four-time champion the series has had.

2024.season: a third title in 2024, and the first back-to-back since 2010
2024.note: Palou won only two races and still took the championship ahead of Colton Herta, Will Power and Scott McLaughlin, becoming the first driver to defend the title since Franchitti did it across 2009, 2010 and 2011.

2023.note: Palou won five races and settled a second title at Portland with a race to spare. He also took pole for the Indianapolis 500 at a record 234.217 mph.

2022.clinched: Laguna Seca, 2022, at the final round
2022.note: Power arrived at the finale with Josef Newgarden and Scott Dixon level on points behind him and needed to finish no worse than third, which he did. He won only one race all year, at Detroit, and earlier in the season had passed Mario Andretti’s all-time record for pole positions.

2021.clinched: Long Beach, 2021, at the final round
2021.note: Palou took his first title by 35 points from Pato O’Ward, with three race wins, and became the first Spanish driver to win a national championship in American open-wheel racing.

2020.clinched: St Petersburg, 2020, at the final round
2020.note: Dixon won four races and beat Josef Newgarden by 16 points at the finale for a sixth title, seventeen years after his first.

2019.clinched: Laguna Seca, 2019, at the final round
2019.note: Newgarden took a second title by 25 points, with four race wins, having led the standings after every race of the season except the Indianapolis 500, which his teammate Simon Pagenaud won.

2018.note: Dixon finished second in the last race to take a fifth title on 678 points, with three race wins.

2017.note: Newgarden needed fourth or better and finished second to take his first title, ahead of Scott Dixon, with four race wins. He was the first American to win the Astor Cup since Ryan Hunter-Reay in 2012.

2016.season: five race wins in 2016, and a first title
2016.note: Pagenaud won five races for Team Penske and finished ahead of his teammate Will Power. Three years later he would win the Indianapolis 500, the first driver born in France to do so since Gaston Chevrolet in 1920.

2015.clinched: the 2015 season, tied on points and settled on race wins
2015.note: Dixon and Juan Pablo Montoya both finished on 556 points, and the title went to Dixon on a count-back of victories, three to two. It is one of two championships in this series decided that way, the other being 2006.

2014.note: Power finished ninth in the last race to take his first title by 62 points from Hélio Castroneves, with three race wins. He had been runner-up in the standings in each of the three previous seasons.

2013.clinched: Auto Club Speedway, 2013, at the final round
2013.note: Dixon finished fifth in the closing race to take a third title on 577 points, with four race wins, ahead of Hélio Castroneves.

2012.clinched: Auto Club Speedway, Fontana, 2012, at the final round
2012.note: Hunter-Reay needed fifth or better once Will Power was penalised, and got it: when Takuma Sato spun on the last lap he avoided the contact and finished fourth, taking the title on 468 points with four race wins. He was the first American champion since Sam Hornish Jr. in 2006.

2011.clinched: Las Vegas, 16 October 2011, at a race that was abandoned
2011.note: Franchitti led Will Power by 18 points going into the finale. On the eleventh lap a fifteen-car accident killed Dan Wheldon, the 2005 champion, who was thrown airborne into a fencepost and died of head injuries. The race was abandoned and the standings reverted to the previous round, which gave Franchitti a fourth title. It is the only championship in this series settled by a race being stopped and not resumed.

2010.note: Franchitti took a third title after Will Power crashed in the closing race, and he won the Indianapolis 500 that year as well, a double nobody repeated until Palou in 2025.

2009.note: Franchitti beat Scott Dixon by eleven points at the finale, with four race wins, in his first season back after a year in NASCAR.

2008.note: Dixon won the last race by 0.0033 seconds, the second-closest finish the series has recorded, and took the title by 30 points from Hélio Castroneves. He won five races that year, and the Indianapolis 500.

2007.note: Franchitti won his first title when Scott Dixon ran out of fuel on the final lap of the closing race. He had won four races including the Indianapolis 500, which was itself shortened by rain.

2006.clinched: Chicagoland, 2006, tied on points and settled on race wins
2006.note: Hornish Jr. and Dan Wheldon finished the season level on points, and the tie went to Hornish on victories, four to two. He had won the Indianapolis 500 that year, and it was Penske’s first championship in this series. The other title decided on a count-back was 2015.

2005.clinched: the 2005 season, settled before the penultimate round
2005.note: Wheldon won a record six races including the Indianapolis 500, where he made the pass with seven laps left to become the first British winner since Graham Hill in 1966, and finished on 628 points. His 102-point lead put the title beyond reach with a race still to run. He was killed at Las Vegas in October 2011, in the accident that ended that season.

2004.season: the 2004 season, in which the champion completed every lap
2004.note: Kanaan won three races and finished on 618 points, and did something no champion here has matched: he completed all 3,305 racing laps of the season, never once failing to see a chequered flag.

2003.note: Dixon won his first title on 507 points with three race wins, ahead of Hélio Castroneves, at 23 and in his first season with Chip Ganassi Racing.

2002.note: Hornish Jr. won five races and took a second consecutive title at the closing race, with eleven top-five finishes across the season.

2001.clinched: the 2001 season, settled before the final round at Texas
2001.note: Hornish Jr. won three races and finished 105 points clear of Buddy Lazier, the defending champion, with a race still to run. At 22 he was the youngest champion the series had had.

2000.note: Lazier finished fourth in the closing race to take the title on 290 points, 18 clear of Scott Goodyear and 33 clear of Eddie Cheever, with three race wins. Four years earlier he had won the Indianapolis 500 with a fractured vertebra, in pain and walking with a cane, in a car fitted with a shock-absorbing seat.

1999.season: three race wins in 1999, and the only top-ten points finish of a career
1999.note: Ray won at Pikes Peak twice and at Dover for Team Menard, and it was the only season of his career in which he finished inside the top ten in the standings. His form fell away sharply afterwards.

1998.season: the 1998 season, and three consecutive wins
1998.note: Bräck took the title on 332 points for A. J. Foyt Enterprises with a run of three straight victories, one of them the 500-kilometre race at Charlotte. The following May he won the Indianapolis 500, the first Swedish driver to do so.

1997.season: the 1997 season, won by a driver who would also win in NASCAR
1997.note: Stewart beat Davey Hamilton to the title for Team Menard across a ten-race schedule, taking his first career win at Pikes Peak where he led all but seven of the 200 laps. He had five retirements that year. He remains the only driver to have won a championship in both IndyCar and NASCAR, adding Cup titles in 2002, 2005 and 2011.

1996.season: the first season, in 1996, which ended in a tie nobody had written a rule for
1996.note: Calkins and Sharp finished the three-race inaugural season level on points, and because no tiebreaker rule existed they were declared joint champions. The calendar was Walt Disney World Speedway, Phoenix and the Indianapolis 500, and points were multiplied by the number of events a driver had entered, with only fifteen drivers contesting all three. The series had been created in the split with CART, and its 25/8 rule reserved Indianapolis places for its own points-scorers, which is why seventeen of the 33 starters at that year’s 500 were rookies. Buddy Lazier won it.
